A Movie a Week 2026 🎞️ - 36/52 Wow, that was so boring, it’s actually quite impressive. Nothing fucking happened. This film didn’t give me anything to give a review about. Empty, hollow, painfully jarring experience. Boring, pointless and unlikable characters. Bad casting (not you De Niro), KAREN IS SUPPOSED TO BE 19 WHEN SHE FIRST APPEARS AND SHE’S CLEARLY PUSHING 40?! Why did they think her relationship with her parents would look natural, as she’s oh soo clearly in an age where she won’t soon even remember her twenties LET ALONE BE LIVING THEM AT THE PRESENT MOMENT?!?!? So many of the dynamics and interactions seemed so out of place due to problems with the casting/acting. Not to mention bunch of the characters looking weird overall; somehow waxy, uncanny even (best example being Karen’s mom) What was the message of this film? Goodfellas had absolutely nothing to say. I found the narration extremely infuriating, since the plot and what there was to be seen with the eye was incredibly clear, I don’t have to hear you guide me through it: ”Here I’m walking on the street. I shoot a guy cause I can. We’re the Goodfellas, the wiseguys. We are baaaad , yeah!” I mean they even dropped the infamous ”this is not like it is in the movies” line. Like really? This is that 4.5 star, unique, outstanding, life-altering cinema for you guys? What the fuck am I missing, this is seriously pissing me off?! I’m tired of hating critically acclaimed films and it’s soon gonna start looking like I’m going out of my way to do so!! Believe me when I tell you, I really wanted to like Goodfellas , but unfortunately my gutfeeling about there not being a unique plot for a mafia film, is starting to prove itself to be true. I’ve now seen ”the big three” of mafia films and Scarface holds its place as the one and only legendary one. There was one (1) ((as in one unit)) (((a total of just one))) scene, where I felt like ”okayyy, we’re getting somewhere!” and even that was over in an instant. On top of that, the events that needed to be shown on screen or given more than a minute of screen time (the first arrest, all the heists) were brushed over like I’ve never seen before. A total mess.

A Movie A Week 2026 - 36/52 "As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster." 4.5 stars?? Really ? This film had nothing to give that I haven't seen before. It goes through the basic tropes of mafia flicks without bringing anything of its own. It lacks the intelligent scheming and plotting of something like "The Godfather" . It lacks the explosive action and entertainment of something like "Scarface" . It lacks the cunning and charismatic protagonists of either. Hell, every single character is completely irredeemable and unlikeable. I get that the main characters in mafia stories are always fated to be bad people, but I didn't care for anyone in this film. Makes it impossible to be invested. That isn't helped by the fact that the lead performance by Ray Liotta is weak. The whole cast all around is strange and unconvincing. Why do we have a 47-year-old Robert DeNiro playing a guy in his late 20s? Why is a supposedly 19-year-old Karen played by a 35 year-old woman? Of course that's gonna cause some disconnect and detachment from the story! And fuck, this is just so boring. We barely see any action unfold. Any big heists that go down are simply narrated to the audience. Nothing that occurs feels impactful in the slightest. Really having a hard time understanding what it is everyone else supposedly sees in this film...

Le casting est excellent et la mise en scène irréprochable. J'interprète ce film comme une réflexion sur l'immoralité. Contrairement à de nombreux films de gangsters, il ne cherche pas véritablement à glorifier ses personnages en leur attribuant des qualités chevaleresques, comme la solidarité ou l'honneur, qui viendraient en quelque sorte compenser leurs actes infâmes. Le film semble au contraire nous dire : regardez donc ce que vous, spectateurs, admirez tant. Pourtant, ce que je reproche à Martin Scorsese, c'est d'avoir choisi une approche extrêmement centrée sur les hommes. Comment peut-on représenter un tel univers en effaçant presque totalement une partie de la population ? Où est l'écosystème social qui entoure cette mafia ? Les femmes sont bien présentes, mais leurs personnages ne sont ni développés ni dotés d'une véritable personnalité, alors même qu'elles semblent constituer l'arrière-plan indispensable de cette structure. Certes, il n'était pas nécessaire de faire d'elles le sujet principal du film (ce n’est semble il pas l’objectif d’origine). Cependant, il aurait été intéressant de leur donner davantage de profondeur : quel regard portent-elles sur ce monde mafieux ? Comment vivent-elles cette proximité avec la violence, le pouvoir et la criminalité ? Ici, elles apparaissent essentiellement comme des objets de désir lorsqu'elles sont jeunes, comme des gardiennes du foyer lorsqu'elles deviennent épouses et mères, ou encore comme des mères âgées et aveugles aux agissements de leurs fils. Toutes, qu'elles soient jeunes femmes ou femmes mariées, semblent n'avoir qu'un seul désir : intégrer l'univers de l'homme mafieux, dangereux mais irrésistiblement fascinant. Nous sommes en plein dans les clichés. Je ne souhaite pas ici condamner de représenter le banditisme, l'immoralité et certaines formes de masculinité toxique (qui malgré cette intention critique, une forme de fascination ou de glorification peut transparaître aux yeux du spectateur dont l’ambiguïté fait la richesse du film, mais aussi sa limite) mais de déplorer avant tout l'absence d'un autre point de vue, qui aurait permis d'enrichir la réflexion. Au final, il appartient à chacun d'interpréter l'œuvre soit comme une représentation de la masculinité, soit comme une critique du masculinisme ; soit comme la mise en scène d'un idéal fantasmé, soit comme une satire destructrice.

Iconic movies that I've put off watching because there is no way they could live up to the hype usually end up impressing me...unfortunately, Goodfellas was an exception to this. While it does a good job immersing you in the world of a mafia movie, and has some memorable characters, I found that it did a surprisingly poor job building consistent relationships between the characters and making the most of its runtime. While the relentless narration and freeze frames got old quick, where the movie lost me is the large time skips, where relationships or situations get better or worse arbitrarily, which lessens the time that we get to see with the characters. I get that the characters are supposed to be despicable, but they're not likable or unlikable enough to be properly invested in. They're consistently shown to be rolling in money, but take unnecessary risks to try to get more...I know the main character has a fifth grade education and isn't meant to be the best or brightest, but he's got nothing going for him. The way his life falls apart isn't in a "train wreck you can't look away from", but instead something I couldn't wait to get over with, given the day it all falls apart for him is the first time in ten years we've checked in with him, and he's making stupid decisions for no reason. The acting was pretty average in my opinion, Pesci and Deniro were the standouts but don't do anything they haven't done in other roles, and the plot beats were fairly predictable, and nothing too shocking. It was just a really long time to spend with characters that I didn't really have any interest or attachment to, due to the lack of depth, nuance, or originality in any of them. There was nothing particularly bad about this movie, and it wasn't actively unenjoyable. There are some really good long shots, and the setting and atmosphere are really solid, there is clearly care and thought put into the filming of this movie. There just wasn't a single moment I can think of that kept me glued to the screen, surprised me, or made me feel anything at all, other than indifference.

Mob films aren’t my thing in general. Scorsese’s style, while often entertaining and extremely well-made, usually leaves me at a crossroads. He may be great at character studies, but he’s far too generous with some of them, especially when they existed in real life. His documentary style approach to scrutinizing bad men has always been misunderstood. I’ve tried to give him grace, but when I research the real story, there’s always a battle between intent and impact. This is praised for its “realism” but they had to sanitize who Henry Hill was to make his story digestible on the big screen. It’s never a good sign if the deplorable subject of your film ultimately benefits from the glamorized and borderline sympathetic worldview that was constructed within it. Scorsese clearly means to show how dark and isolating the gangster life is, but that comes at the cost of heightening its allure for entertainment’s sake. I have reserved opinions on whether or not we can fault filmmakers for things like this. When it comes to fictional characters, it’s a different story. I’m obviously not going to blame Martin for that assassin who took inspiration from Taxi Driver. But Henry Hill was a real bad person who eventually profited off his reputation from this film. Still, I can admit that the ending of this pretty much condemns the man as one who refuses to change. Probably the most realistic part of the whole movie. Hey! While they’re not always my cup of tea, I don’t have anything against cautionary tales of reproachable men. However, it always bugs me when male directors feed into the fantasy part too much when the real life story is something even darker and more tragic. Scorsese tows that line way too much for my comfort.

Ray Liotta’s voiceover functions as a darkly intoxicating tour guide through a world where loyalty is a transactional facade and violence is merely an occupational hazard. Sé que esto probablemente para el tipico filmbro que sólo considera cine las películas de Nolan, Scorsese y Tarantino, sea un crimen peor que cualquiera de los que aparecen en la película, pero... para gustos, colores. Reconozco que "Goodfellas" está increíblemente bien hecha (para la época, at least). Scorsese sabe exactamente cómo contar esta historia y lo hace de un modo espectacular, la banda sonora es perfecta y el reparto está absolutamente desatado, ya que Ray Liotta, Robert De Niro y Joe Pesci están increíbles. Entonces, ¿dónde esta el problema? Pues la cosa esta en que puedo apreciar todo lo que hace bien Scorsese en esta película sin haber conseguido conectar demasiado con la historia. Tal vez soy el tipo de persona que necesita empatizar al menos con algún personaje para que pueda conectar con una película, pero es que, sinceramente, me daba exactamente igual el destino de todos los personajes. De hecho, estaba deseando que acabarán todos muertos o en la cárcel. Además, el intento del final de vendernos a Henry como si fuera un héroe... girl, whatever. La película consigue que entres en el mundo de la mafia y que durante un rato parezca incluso atractivo: el dinero, las fiestas, los trajes, el poder... hasta que poco a poco todo empieza a desmoronarse, pero su ritmo y su duración hicieron que por momentos se me hiciera bastante cuesta arriba. No digo que "Goodfellas" sea mala, ni mucho menos. Entiendo perfectamente por qué es considerada un clásico y por qué ha influido tantísimo en el cine posterior. Simplemente creo no hemos conectado. A lo mejor es demasiado straight white boy cinema para mi. En conclusión, "Goodfellas" está muy bien, pero tampoco nos vengamos arriba, porque no es una película que me haya cambiado la vida.

‘Your murderers come with smiles.’ Raucous humour and horrifying violence are not mutually exclusive in GoodFellas , the protagonists of Martin Scorsese’s gangster opus continually laughing through acts of incredible brutality. This tonal paradox that underscores the film provides unique insight into the strange culture of the American mafia, a world in which tales of death and destruction are reduced to bawdy anecdotes shared around the barroom. Murder is such a casual occurrence within this subculture that the characters are able to discuss chopping up a body as if they were talking about the weather, the likes of Tommy and Jimmy cracking jokes with Maury right up until the moment they drive a screwdriver through his skull. The main trio even share an inside joke about the body currently stewing in the trunk while eating dinner with Tommy’s mother, this kind of gallows humour arguably used as a defence mechanism to distract from the horror they have just inflicted upon another human being. It is a unique kind of sociopathy in which their responses to the injustices of the world are all the wrong way around, the characters reacting to the owner of a restaurant being hit over the head with a glass bottle not with outrage but amusement. Certain characters even go so far to use humour as an intimidation tactic, the character of Tommy blurring the lines between affection and hostility for his own pleasure during the infamous ‘funny how?’ scene. The ability to lie, cheat, and steal through a permanent grin is the calling card of a professional sociopath in Scorsese’s murderous masterpiece, the filmmaker walking the line between horror and hilarity with a skill few artists are able to achieve.

There’s not much that can be said about this film that hasn’t been said a million times already. It’s one of the few films out there that 100% deserves all the praise and hype it gets and is one that always gets a little bit better every time I see it. At this point, it’s more of a comfort movie for me than anything. Everyone here is at the top of their game, like I could gush on and on about how much I love Ray Liotta, Robert De Niro, Lorraine Bracco, and so on but we’d be here for hours. With that said, the clear standout from the cast is Joe Pesci, who is absolutely fucking electric in this. Every line spoken from this man’s mouth is pure comedy gold, yet he’s such a loose cannon that he can turn you from laughing to terrified in a matter of seconds. That Oscar was completely deserved. The structure of this film is also something that I can’t really get enough of, and to some extent, the same could be said for Scorsese (Wolf of Wall Street, The Irishman, etc.). I just love how much it builds up the mobster life in the first act, showing all the excesses that drew Henry into it in the first place. Then, the second act comes, you start seeing the cracks show, and you really get a bleak picture of how psychotic, deranged, and destructive these people are. As the third act arrives, everything falls apart in a chaotic way that puts you on edge until the very end. I think this structure is not only a great feat in writing but also editing, which can be attributed to Thelma Schoonmaker’s genius work. The entire sequence with the helicopter still gives me so much anxiety, and almost all of that is because of the frantic way it’s edited. From a director with such an iconic filmography, this film really stands out as a timeless classic that I think I could watch endlessly for the rest of my life.

The whole context is spectacular a masterclass in camera angles, lighting, and contrast. Lorraine Bracco is flawless as well. While she shines even brighter in The Sopranos, she anchors crucial moments here, like that iconic tracking shot with Ray Liotta that provides an unreal level of immersion.
